subtitle: A Kashmiri Poet in Ajmer and the Long Shadow of Prithviraj

panels.shot: epic three-quarter view, Jayanaka seated with palm-leaf manuscript before a dim Ajmer palace, half in lamplight, half in shadow
panels.action: Jayanaka, robed Kashmiri poet, sits cross-legged over palm leaves, stylus poised, Ajmer’s fort walls looming behind him under a troubled sky.

dialogue.text: In Ajmer’s fading light, Kashmiri poet Jayanaka writes Prithviraj’s glory—then falls silent before the king’s final battle. Why is his broken song the source we trust?

i18n.hi: अजमेर की ढलती रोशनी में कश्मीरी कवि जयनाक पृथ्वीराज का गुणगान लिखता है—फिर अंतिम युद्ध से पहले ही चुप हो जाता है। उसकी टूटी कविता पर हम इतना क्यों भरोसा करते हैं?

panels.shot: slow push-in from high-angle, scholar’s cell in Ajmer palace
panels.action: Inside a quiet chamber, Jayanaka bends over a low desk, palm leaves stacked, an oil lamp flickering as distant drums echo from the city.

dialogue.text: Around 1191, as Ajmer’s king rides to war, a Kashmiri scholar in his court begins a Sanskrit mahakavya: Prithviraja-Vijaya, the Victory of Prithviraj.

i18n.hi: लगभग 1191 में, जब अजमेर का राजा युद्ध पर निकलता है, उसके दरबार का कश्मीरी विद्वान एक संस्कृत महाकाव्य शुरू करता है: ‘पृथ्वीराज-विजय’, यानी पृथ्वीराज की विजय।

panels.shot: medium shot, Jayanaka in profile, Pushkar imagined in background as a shimmering vision
panels.action: Jayanaka pauses, eyes lifted as if seeing Pushkar’s sacred lake in his mind, while script lines flow across a palm leaf before him.

dialogue.text: He frames Prithviraj as born to restore dharma at Pushkar, where Ghaznavid raids had scarred shrines around the holy lake. Theology and memory fold into his verse.

i18n.hi: वह पृथ्वीराज को धर्म की पुनर्स्थापना के लिए जन्मा बताता है—पुष्कर में, जहाँ गज़नवी हमलों ने पवित्र झील के चारों ओर मंदिरों पर घाव छोड़े थे। उसकी कविता में देव-विचार और यादें घुल-मिल जाते हैं।

panels.shot: low-angle close-up on stylus and palm leaf, faint superimposed silhouettes of Chahamana rulers behind
panels.action: Jayanaka’s hand carves neat letters as ghostlike images of Arnoraja, Someshvara, and Prithviraj rise behind him like a lineage in mist.

dialogue.text: From genealogy and lakes carved by Arnoraja, to Someshvara’s years in Gujarat, he anchors his poem in the Chahamana line and real places the court knew.

i18n.hi: वंशावली से लेकर अर्णोराज द्वारा खुदवाए सरोवरों तक, और गुजरात में सोमेश्वर के वर्षों तक—वह अपने गीत को चौहान वंश और दरबार को जान-पहचान वाली जगहों में गाड़ देता है।

panels.shot: extreme close-up on Jayanaka’s thoughtful eyes, faint lines of multiple scripts around him
panels.action: Jayanaka gazes at a leaf covered in Sanskrit while ghostly letters in other scripts hover around his head, hinting at Prithviraj’s reputed languages.

dialogue.text: He praises Prithviraj as mastering many tongues—an image of a king who could hear traders, priests, and envoys in their own words.

i18n.hi: वह पृथ्वीराज को कई भाषाओं का उस्ताद बताता है—ऐसा राजा जो व्यापारियों, पुरोहितों और दूतों की बात उनकी अपनी जुबान में सुन सके।

panels.shot: wide shot, palace hall with Prithviraj on throne and a dark foreign envoy before him, seen from behind Jayanaka
panels.action: From the edge of an audience hall, Jayanaka watches Prithviraj on his lion-backed throne as a Ghurid envoy, drawn harsh and hunched, stands before him.

dialogue.text: One day, an envoy came from Muhammad of Ghor. In Jayanaka’s telling, the man is ghastly, foul-voiced—a shadow at the edge of a radiant court.

i18n.hi: एक दिन मुहम्मद गौरी की ओर से एक दूत आया। जयनाक की नजर में वह डरावना, गंदी आवाज वाला—चमकते दरबार की किनारी पर पड़ी एक काली परछाईं।

panels.shot: close-up, split-screen style: on one side the envoy twisted and coarse; on the other Prithviraj serene and upright
panels.action: The image splits: the envoy’s face contorted and coarse on one side, Prithviraj calm and straight-backed on the other, Jayanaka’s stylus scratching between them.

dialogue.speaker: jayanaka
dialogue.text: Let the king shine brighter as his enemy grows small.

i18n.hi: दुश्मन जितना छोटा हो, राजा उतना ज्यादा चमके।

panels.shot: dramatic match-cut, Persian scribe’s hand writing in a different script on paper, Ajmer imagined in distance
panels.action: A Persian scribe’s hand, in another city, glides over paper with elegant curves of script, Ajmer’s fort faint in the far background.

dialogue.text: Yet Hasan Nizami, writing Taj-ul-Maasir in Persian, remembers a Ghurid envoy as refined and graceful—his words polished for his own patron.

i18n.hi: लेकिन फ़ारसी में ताज-उल-मासिर लिखने वाले हसन निज़ामी को एक घुरीद दूत नफ़ीस और शालीन याद है—अपने ख़ुद के सरपरस्त के लिए सजी-सँवरी जुबान।

panels.shot: wide, two scribes back-to-back in different worlds: Jayanaka in Ajmer and the Persian chronicler in a Ghurid court
panels.action: Jayanaka and a Persian chronicler sit back-to-back in separate chambers, each surrounded by their own rulers and priests, their scripts glowing in different hues.

dialogue.text: Two courts. Two patrons. Two pens. The same envoy becomes villain in one language, courtly in another. Bias is not hidden; it shines on the page.

i18n.hi: दो दरबार। दो सरपरस्त। दो कलम। वही दूत एक भाषा में खलनायक, दूसरी में सलीकेदार। पक्षपात छुपा नहीं, पन्नों पर चमकता दिखता है।

panels.shot: medium shot, Jayanaka weighing two palm leaves in his hands like scales
panels.action: Jayanaka sits with two sets of manuscripts, one Sanskrit, one imagined in Persian calligraphy, held like scales before him as he frowns in thought.

dialogue.text: Modern historians read both, note what each saw, and ask: where do they agree, where do they bend the light for their own king?

i18n.hi: आज के इतिहासकार दोनों को पढ़ते हैं, देखते हैं किसने क्या देखा, और पूछते हैं: कहाँ वे सहमत हैं, और कहाँ अपने-अपने राजा के लिए रोशनी मोड़ देते हैं?

panels.shot: slow push-in, Jayanaka writing intensely while outside distant riders and dust hint at looming war
panels.action: Jayanaka writes swiftly, shoulders tense, as beyond his window horsemen ride and dust rises, the sense of the coming second battle of Tarain hanging unspoken.

dialogue.text: As war with Ghor tightens, Prithviraja-Vijaya moves towards a clash it never reaches. The poem breaks off before Tarain’s second battle.

i18n.hi: जब गौरी से जंग कसती जाती है, ‘पृथ्वीराज-विजय’ जिस टकराव की ओर बढ़ता है, वहाँ कभी पहुँचता ही नहीं। कविता तराइन की दूसरी लड़ाई से पहले ही टूट जाती है।

panels.shot: close-up on unfinished manuscript: last written line clear, then blank palm leaves stretching ahead
panels.action: The last line of the manuscript ends crisply, followed by a stack of blank leaves, Jayanaka’s stylus lying still beside them.

dialogue.text: Perhaps conquest scattered the court; perhaps the poet fled or fell. We do not know why his voice stops, only that silence follows Prithviraj’s last campaigns.

i18n.hi: शायद फ़तह ने दरबार बिखेर दिया; शायद कवि भागा या मारा गया। हमें बस इतना मालूम है कि उसकी आवाज़ थम जाती है—और पृथ्वीराज की आखिरी लड़ाइयों के बाद केवल सन्नाटा बचता है।

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot, Ajmer’s skyline fading, new cities and libraries appearing over centuries
panels.action: Ajmer’s fort slowly dims as layers of new cities, Jain monasteries, and distant sultanate domes rise, manuscripts piling in different scripts across the scene.

dialogue.text: Later centuries add Jain prabandhas, like Merutunga’s Prabandha-Chintamani, and heroic poems like Hammira Mahakavya—rich, but a hundred years or more removed.

i18n.hi: बाद की सदियों में मेरुतुंग का ‘प्रबंध-चिंतामणि’ जैसे जैन प्रबंध, और ‘हम्मीर महाकाव्य’ जैसे वीर-गीत जुड़ते हैं—घने, पर सौ साल से भी ज्यादा बाद के।

panels.shot: medium shot of a bard at a rural fire reciting Prithviraj Raso, villagers listening
panels.action: In a village courtyard centuries later, a bard stands by a fire, reciting lines as listeners lean in, the legend of Prithviraj swirling in the night.

dialogue.text: Prithviraj Raso grows as oral epic and court romance—shaping memory and pride—but for historians it is song, not chronicle.

i18n.hi: ‘पृथ्वीराज रासो’ मौखिक महाकाव्य और दरबारी प्रेमकथा बनकर फैलता जाता है—याद और शान गढ़ता है—पर इतिहासकारों के लिए वह गीत है, तिथी-पत्र नहीं।

panels.shot: scholarly table top-down: modern historian’s hands, open books of Jayanaka, Persian chronicles, Jain texts, and Raso marked with notes
panels.action: On a modern desk, open editions of Prithviraja-Vijaya, a Persian chronicle, a Jain prabandha, and Prithviraj Raso lie side by side, margins crowded with careful notes.

dialogue.text: Today, source-critics like Cynthia Talbot rank them: Jayanaka and near-contemporary Persian accounts first; later Jain and Sanskrit works next; the Raso as cultural memory.

i18n.hi: आज सिन्थिया टैलबॉट जैसे स्रोत-परीक्षक इन्हें क्रम में रखते हैं: पहले जयनाक और लगभग समकालीन फ़ारसी वृतांत; फिर बाद के जैन और संस्कृत ग्रंथ; और रासो को सांस्कृतिक स्मृति की तरह।

panels.shot: intimate close-up, Jayanaka looking directly toward viewer, lamplight on his face, manuscripts behind
panels.action: Jayanaka turns from his manuscript as if seeing across time, lamplight tracing the lines on his face, rolled palm leaves stacked behind him.

dialogue.text: His poem gives us genealogy, Pushkar’s scars, Karpuradevi’s place, a multilingual king, and that charged envoy—details no later legend could invent as precisely.

i18n.hi: उसकी कविता हमें वंशावली, पुष्कर के घाव, कर्पूरादेवी का स्थान, बहुभाषी राजा और वह तना हुआ दूत देती है—ऐसी बारीकियाँ जो बाद की कथाएँ इतनी सटीक गढ़ ही नहीं सकतीं।

panels.shot: wide, Jayanaka seated amid floating fragments of different accounts, each glowing with distinct color and script
panels.action: Jayanaka sits at the center as fragments of Sanskrit, Persian, Jain, and bardic verses drift around him, each a different color, none touching but all visible.

dialogue.text: Each source is a voice with its own loyalties. History begins when we ask what each could see, what each wanted, and where their visions cross.

i18n.hi: हर स्रोत अपनी वफ़ादारियों वाली एक आवाज़ है। इतिहास तब शुरू होता है जब हम पूछते हैं: कौन क्या देख सकता था, क्या चाहता था, और जहाँ उनकी दृष्टियाँ एक-दूसरे से मिलती हैं।

panels.shot: final slow pull-back, from manuscript to starry sky over Ajmer and Pushkar
panels.action: The camera pulls back from the manuscript of Prithviraja-Vijaya, through Ajmer and Pushkar’s landscape, into a starry sky where faint lines of text shimmer like constellations.

dialogue.text: Jayanaka’s broken song reminds us: history is not the loudest tale, but the one whose sources we weigh—and honesty begins where the evidence runs out.

i18n.hi: जयनाक का टूटा गीत याद दिलाता है: इतिहास सबसे ऊँची चीख नहीं, वो कथा है जिसके स्रोत हम तौलते हैं—और सच्चाई वहाँ से शुरू होती है जहाँ सबूत खत्म हो जाते हैं।

title_i18n.en: Jayanaka and the Sources We Trust

subtitle_i18n.en: A Kashmiri Poet in Ajmer and the Long Shadow of Prithviraj
subtitle_i18n.hi: अजमेर में कश्मीरी कवि और पृथ्वीराज की लंबी परछाईं
